caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Sierra Leone's debt was reset by HIPC completion in 2006: from 61.9% of GDP it fell to 22.3% by 2013, the series low, as iron ore revenues boomed. The Ebola crisis, the 2014-16 iron ore crash, and persistent deficits rebuilt it: 45.1% projected for 2025, roughly double the post-relief low but still moderate. The debt is mostly concessional, and IMF assessments judge the risk of distress moderate. The deeper issue is revenue: with one of the world's lowest tax takes, even 45% of GDP strains servicing capacity, and the government has repeatedly resorted to expensive domestic borrowing.
inflation_management: Sierra Leone's inflation was contained at 4-8% from 2008 to 2015, then the Ebola aftermath and currency depreciation pushed it to 18.2% in 2017. It moderated to 11-16% through 2021 before the 2022-23 crisis: the leone collapsed and inflation surged to 27.2% in 2022 and a series high of 47.7% in 2023. Aggressive tightening and a 2022 redenomination (cutting three zeros) helped: inflation fell to 28.4% in 2024 and a projected 7.6% in 2025. The central bank has no formal inflation target and limited credibility; the leone's chronic weakness means every external shock becomes a domestic price shock.

key_events.event: HIPC completion-point relief cut debt to about 22% of GDP; iron ore boom began.
Ebola epidemic killed thousands and devastated the economy.
Julius Maada Bio won the presidency (2018); IMF program resumed.
COVID-19; debt climbed past 45% of GDP.
Leone collapse pushed inflation to 47.7%, the series high; currency redenominated.
Bio won disputed re-election (June 2023); inflation fell to a projected 7.6% in 2025.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued IMF-anchored stabilization with inflation in single digits and debt near 45% of GDP. Upside comes from iron ore and rutile revenues if managed well; downside is the familiar cycle of currency crises forcing inflation spikes. Uncertainty is moderate: institutions are weak but the 2023 election, though disputed, did not derail the macro framework.
